story: The land here is young and soft. It was sea floor about a million years ago, sandstone and mudstone, papa, and water has since cut it into sharp ridges, deep gorges, sheer cliffs and a maze of V-shaped valleys. The Whanganui River runs through the middle of it, the longest continually navigable river in New Zealand, although its bed and waters are not part of the park. After heavy rain, waterfalls pour off the gorge walls.

The park protects one of the largest remaining tracts of lowland forest in the North Island: podocarps and broadleaf trees, kāmahi and tawa, rimu, tōtara and kahikatea, with black beech on the dry ridges and northern rātā making a spectacular display in midsummer. It is home to the largest population of North Island brown kiwi in New Zealand, several thousand birds, and whio, blue duck, live on the clean, fast rivers. Eighteen species of native fish live in the river.

Māori used the river and its tributaries for trade and travel at least 600 years ago, and Te Āti Haunui-a-Pāpārangi cultivated its terraces and built pā on the heights, so many along the upper river that they were called the plaited fibres of Hinengākau. Every bend and rapid has its kaitiaki, its guardian. In 2017 Parliament recognised Te Awa Tupua, the river from the mountains to the sea, as an indivisible, living whole and a legal person.

Missionaries came in the 1840s, and from 1891 riverboats carried passengers, mail and freight between Whanganui and Taumarunui. After the First World War returned soldiers were given farms in the Mangapurua and Kaiwhakauka valleys, but erosion, floods and poor roads defeated them; by 1944 every family had gone, leaving a concrete bridge with no road. The national park was gazetted on 6 December 1986.
howItWorks: Whanganui National Park is run by the Department of Conservation (DOC). DOC says plainly that there are no fees for entry into the park; under the National Parks Act 1980 the public has freedom of entry and access, and what you pay for is a hut, a campsite, or a guide, canoe hire or jet boat from a local business. There are few easy road access points, and on the river and most tracks there is no cell phone coverage, so carry a distress beacon.

The Whanganui Journey is one of DOC's Great Walks, the only one that is a canoe trip. In the Great Walks season, 1 October to 30 April, its huts and campsites must be booked and paid in advance; from 1 May to 30 September they cannot be booked and are first come, first served, with hut fees paid by Backcountry Hut Pass or hut tickets and campsite fees in cash at the fee boxes at Ohinepane or Whakahoro. Away from the river, the Matemateāonga Track has serviced huts; DOC charges $25 an adult a night for most serviced huts and nothing for basic huts.

This is a cultural landscape as much as a natural one. Tīeke Kāinga is both a DOC hut and a working marae, run jointly by Te Whānau o Tīeke and DOC, with its own tikanga; Tamatea's Cave on the river is wāhi tapu and must not be entered. DOC asks visitors to avoid alcohol and smoking on the river and at Tīeke. Dogs and other pets are not allowed in the park, fires are not permitted, and you may not hunt within the river trench.

sightNotes.poi-nz-whanganui-bridge-to-nowhere: A concrete bridge nearly 40 metres above the Mangapurua Stream, opened in 1936 for a soldier settlement that had already failed. A 40-minute walk from Mangapurua Landing.
sightNotes.poi-nz-whanganui-mangapurua-landing: The river landing for the Bridge to Nowhere, reached by canoe or jet boat. The rock is very slippery when wet and often crowded with boats.
sightNotes.poi-nz-whanganui-matemateaonga-track: A 42-kilometre tramp of three to five days along an old Māori trail and settlers' dray road on the crest of the Matemateāonga Range, ending at the river.
sightNotes.poi-nz-whanganui-whakaihuwaka-maunga: A 732-metre summit off the Matemateāonga Track with a view of three national parks: Whanganui, Te Papa-Kura-o-Taranaki and Tongariro.
sightNotes.poi-nz-whanganui-atene-skyline-track: A 12.5-kilometre ridge walk from the Whanganui River Road around Puketapu hill and a cut-off meander of the river, rising to 572 metres at Taumata Trig.

chronology.text: Māori are using the Whanganui River and its tributaries for trade and travel, at least 600 years ago.
Missionaries arrive, and chapels are built at villages along the river.
A regular riverboat service begins carrying passengers, mail and freight between Whanganui and Taumarunui.
The first returned servicemen take up soldier-settlement farms in the Mangapurua Valley.
The steel-reinforced concrete bridge over the Mangapurua Stream opens, replacing a wooden swing bridge of 1919.
The last settlers leave the Mangapurua Valley after the government stops maintaining the road.
Whanganui National Park is gazetted on 6 December; it opens officially in February 1987.
Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui River Claims Settlement) Act receives assent on 20 March, recognising the river as a living whole and a legal person.

safety: Do not set off if the river is flooding, rising or forecast to flood, and tie your canoe up securely at night. You will not be charged for an extra night spent waiting for the river to drop.
Wear a life jacket at all times on the water. Unguided paddlers should be confident swimmers with canoe experience, fit enough for six to seven hours a day, over ten, and at least two in a group.
Jet boats use the river. Keep to the true right where you can, stop or back-paddle as one approaches, and turn your canoe at right angles to its wake.
There is no cell phone coverage on the river or most tracks. Carry a distress beacon, and treat or boil all water from huts, campsites and streams.
Follow the Land Safety Code from DOC and the NZ Mountain Safety Council: choose the right trip, understand the weather, pack warm clothes and extra food, share your plans, and look after each other.
regulations: No dogs or other pets in the park.
No fires in the park; on the Whanganui Journey follow all fire restrictions and light no open fires.
Camp only at designated campsites, and book huts and campsites on the Journey in the Great Walks season.
Do not enter Tamatea's Cave or other wāhi tapu, and follow the tikanga at Tīeke Kāinga, where alcohol and smoking are to be avoided.
No hunting within the river trench; keep soap and detergent out of the water.

weather: The climate is relatively mild all year, but cold temperatures and heavy rain are common and the weather can change fast. Most people come between December and Easter, when river levels are lower and the days long; northern rātā flower in midsummer. From May to September the river is often high, the water very cold and the weather wet, with short daylight hours. The river can rise overnight even when it is not raining where you are: if it is rising or in flood, stay at your hut or campsite. Wasps are common from January to May.
directions: The park lies in the central North Island, between Taumarunui to the north and Whanganui to the south, with the small settlements of Pipiriki, Ohinepane and Whakahoro as the main gateways to the river. Roads lead into the park from all directions, some to the tracks and some to the river. Regular buses run to Taumarunui and Whanganui, and several companies run shuttles to the track ends and move cars for paddlers. Pipiriki is about 76 kilometres up the Whanganui River Road from Whanganui, or 27 kilometres from Raetihi on State Highway 4 by the Pipiriki–Raetihi Road. The Atene Skyline Track starts on the Whanganui River Road, 36 kilometres from Whanganui.
